lesson.title: Conducting World War I
lesson.summary: How governments waged total war, how new weapons created stalemate, and how colonial peoples were drawn into the fighting.
learningGoals: Explain how governments used a variety of methods to conduct war.
lesson.bigIdea: World War I was a total war in which governments mobilized entire societies and empires, and industrial weapons produced unprecedented casualties.
lesson.context: Generals expected a short war. Instead, industrial weapons created a long, deadly stalemate.

blocks.text: In total war, governments directed industry, rationed food, and drafted millions. Women took jobs in factories and transportation. Propaganda portrayed enemies as monstrous and urged civilians to support the war.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Because the war required vast amounts of weapons and soldiers, governments took control of economies, which drew women into new kinds of work.

sections.title: Trenches and new weapons

blocks.text: Machine guns and artillery forced armies into trenches on the Western Front. Attacks across open ground killed hundreds of thousands. Poison gas, used on a large scale from 1915, and tanks, from 1916, did not end the stalemate.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: New weapons did not bring quick victory. Most new technologies added to the killing without breaking the stalemate.

sections.takeaway: Industrial weapons made defense stronger than attack, producing a war of attrition.

sections.title: Empires at war

blocks.text: About 1.3 million Indian soldiers and laborers served Britain. France recruited troops from West Africa, North Africa, and Indochina, and China sent about 140,000 laborers to France.
Many colonial soldiers expected rewards for their service. Disappointment after the war fed demands for self-government.

sections.takeaway: Colonial participation in the war strengthened demands for independence.

vocabulary.definition: A war in which governments mobilize entire economies and populations and civilians become part of the war effort.
Information, often biased or misleading, spread by governments to shape public opinion.
Long ditches dug by armies for protection, which produced a deadly stalemate on the Western Front in World War I.
